newsitem.title: USA: U.S. June home sales seen down but still healthy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. June home sales seen down but still healthy.

text.p: Ebullient consumer confidence and lower mortgage rates were sure to have supported existing home sales at a healthy level in June, despite expectations that the existing home sales may have taken a slight dip.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expected June existing home sales data would show sales declined to 4.19 million annualized from May's 4.24 million. While the consensus calls for a slight decline, economists agree that a level above four million signals that the nation's housing industry is healthy.
The June existing home sales data will be released on Friday at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
"A number above four million indicates a very sound housing market," said Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Bank Inc.
Improved employment and a more upbeat consumer are bolstering demand for housing, analysts said.
"High consumer confidence and firm employment" are behind the increased demand, said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors.
"Consumer confidence is at an all-time high and economic growth continues at a modest pace," said Frank Nothaft, deputy chief economist at Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp.
Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, agreed, noting that the stock market's health has also contributed to demand for housing.
"The economy continues to add jobs and the stock market is creating wealth that is creating trade up-buying," said Taylor.
The supply of existing homes, economists said, will be closely watched.
"We will look at the month's inventory number closely," said Taylor, pointing out that inventories of existing homes fell to a 6.7-month supply from 6.9 months in May.
Taylor warned that if inventories rise, existing homes will exhibit the first signs of a slowdown in the housing market.
"My concern is that the gradually building supply of existing housing is not perfectly matched to the needs of the trade-up buyer," Taylor added.
When it comes to supply, Taylor said he believes that continued declines in inventories will show that existing homes are becoming better matched to consumer demand.
Conversely, "if inventories shoot up, it may be the first sign of a generally slowing housing market," said Taylor.
Taylor asserted that mortgage rates are moderating and thus are providing less of a hindrance to so-called trade-up buyers.

But, participants pointed out that 60-percent of the existing housing sales recorded in the June report are contract closings. This implies, Chan said, that the data are a lagging indicator, rather than a current indicator.
Reaser acknowledged this as well, noting that the current low-rate environment may ensure that demand for housing will remain strong for the remainder of 1997.
